title: Hanukkah: Maoz Tzur
hook: a medieval song sung after lighting, recalling many rescues

segments.voice: Yesterday, pirsumei nisa, the lights placed where passers-by can see. Your line was show the light. Did you tell someone your good news? Today, what people sing once the lights are lit. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

The candles are lit. The blessings are said. Kids are already eyeing the doughnuts. And then, in many homes, before anyone moves, someone starts a song. Plenty of people know the tune who don't know most of the words; they hum through the middle and come back loud for the end. Many families sing only the first verse. But it has six, and if you read them all, you find it isn't only a song about Hanukkah. It's a song about a lot of nights like this one.
screen: `THE CANDLES ARE LIT.` → `EVERYONE KNOWS THE TUNE.` → `SIX VERSES, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: The song is called Maoz Tzur. Maoz means stronghold, a fortress. Tzur means rock. The Torah uses rock as a name for God; in the old Jewish translation, Moses sings, "The Rock, His work is perfect." So the song opens by calling God the fortress-rock of my salvation. Who wrote it? The poet signed it in a way medieval Hebrew poets liked: the first letters of the first five verses spell a name, Mordechai. Nobody knows for certain who this Mordechai was. Now the verses. The first looks forward to a rebuilt Temple. The second remembers slavery in Egypt, and the way out. The third, the exile to Babylon, and the return after seventy years. The fourth, Haman, who wanted to destroy the Jews of Persia, and the story we'll meet at Purim. Only the fifth gets to the Greeks, the Hasmoneans, and the jar of oil. And the sixth, likely added later, asks for one more rescue, in the poet's own time. So Hanukkah, in this song, is one link in a chain. Danger, then rescue. Danger, then rescue. People sang it in places where the danger was not ancient history. The English version some families sing, Rock of Ages, is a loose adaptation rather than a translation. And Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other songs, or other tunes. The words that travel everywhere are the first two: fortress, rock.
screen: `MAOZ: FORTRESS. TZUR: ROCK.` · `SIGNED BY A POET, MORDECHAI.` · `EGYPT, BABYLON, HAMAN, GREECE.` · `ONE LINK IN A CHAIN.` · then, large: `ROCK OF AGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one song of rescue. Before the bell, think of a song that has carried you through something: a hard year, a long drive, a loss. It doesn't have to be religious. Hum the first line, quietly, or just hear it in your head. Then think of one rescue in your own story, a time you got through. Let the song and the memory sit together. Breathe with them. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. Dedication, and in Maoz Tzur, one rescue in a long chain of rescues, sung after the lights. Today's word.
Your line: rock of ages. Today, when something feels shaky, hum your song of rescue and remember one time you got through. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi homes, the family sings Maoz Tzur together after lighting the Hanukkah candles each night, usually the first verse; Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other hymns or Psalm 30.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maoz Tzur is a Hanukkah song.
what it means: it's a song of many rescues, with Hanukkah as one link in the chain.
what a scholar hears: an acrostic signed Mordechai, a poet no one can identify for certain; the sixth verse is likely a later addition.

notes: Deuteronomy 32:4 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

Acrostic: first letters of the first five stanzas spell Mordechai; author's identity unknown, commonly dated to 13th-century Germany. Sixth stanza (Chasof zero'a) often considered a later addition. Verify.

English 'Rock of Ages' adaptation attributed to Marcus Jastrow and Gustav Gottheil (19th century); not quoted. The Ashkenazi tune is often traced to a German folk or chorale melody; hedged with 'probably'.
Sephardi practice (other hymns, Psalm 30) simplified; check.

Editor review (y2 651-668 pass): cut uncited dates (thirteenth-century Germany, 'for centuries', the nineteenth-century English version) and the claim the tune is borrowed from a German melody; 'everyone knows the tune' and 'most families' softened; 'isn't really a song about Hanukkah at all' corrected to 'isn't only', since verse five is about Hanukkah.
